Sample Size for Equivalence or Noninferiority of a Linear Contrast

Source: R/ss_power_equivalence_c.R
ss_power_equivalence_c.Rd

Computes the smallest sample size (per group, or the number of units in a paired design) at which the two one-sided tests procedure (Schuirmann, 1987) for a linear contrast \(\psi = \sum_j c_j \mu_j\), or the companion one-sided noninferiority test, attains a desired power. Power is computed exactly through power_equivalence_c. This is the declaration-probability route to planning; the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) route, which targets the confidence interval width directly, is ss_aipe_c, and the two answer the same question whenever true_contrast = 0 and the width target is calibrated to the bounds.

Usage

ss_power_equivalence_c(
  c_weights = NULL,
  true_sd,
  contrast_lower = NULL,
  contrast_upper = NULL,
  true_contrast = 0,
  desired_power = 0.85,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  side = c("equivalence", "noninferiority"),
  design = c("independent", "paired")
)

Arguments

c_weights

The contrast weights, required for design = "independent". The weights must sum to zero with the positive weights summing to 1 and the negative weights to -1, so that the bounds are on the raw scale of the response. Leave NULL for design = "paired", where the weights are already in the per-unit contrast scores.

true_sd

For design = "independent", the anticipated error standard deviation (the square root of the mean square error). For design = "paired", the anticipated standard deviation of the per-unit contrast scores (for two conditions, of the difference scores). It is \(\sigma\) in the formulas below.

contrast_lower, contrast_upper

Bounds on the raw scale of the response, each positive; the equivalence region is \((-\delta_L, +\delta_U)\), where \(\delta_L\) is contrast_lower and \(\delta_U\) is contrast_upper. For side = "equivalence", contrast_upper is required and contrast_lower defaults to it (symmetric bounds). For side = "noninferiority", the test is against \(-\delta_L\) alone, so contrast_lower is the argument to give; a call that gives only the upper bound uses it as the margin.

true_contrast

The population contrast (\(\psi\)) the design should be able to detect as equivalent (or noninferior). Default 0. For equivalence it must lie strictly inside the bounds; for noninferiority, strictly above \(-\delta_L\). The farther true_contrast sits from the center of the region, the larger the required sample size.

desired_power

The target probability of declaring equivalence (or noninferiority) at true_contrast. Default 0.85, matching ss_power_contrast.

alpha_level

One-sided significance level for each test. Default 0.05.

side

"equivalence" (default) or "noninferiority".

design

"independent" (default) for groups of different units sharing one pooled error term, or "paired" for a contrast measured within each unit, analyzed as the mean of the per-unit contrast scores (see power_equivalence_c).

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value. For design = "independent" the rows are necessary_n_per_group (the recommended sample size of each group the contrast involves), total_N (the number of units the design needs, \(J \times n\) for the \(J\) groups named by c_weights), and actual_power (the exact power achieved at the recommendation). For design = "paired" the rows are necessary_N and actual_power: each condition is observed on every unit, so the answer is the number of units, which is the total sample size, and there is no per-group size to report beside it. The row is named for the quantity it holds; it is the value power_equivalence_c takes as N, as necessary_n_per_group is the value it takes as n_per_group. The result carries the dmar_ss_power class, so tidy and glance summarize it in broom convention; tidy() reports the planned size (per group, or the number of units) and the power in the same columns for both designs.

Details

Design. Planning for independent groups assumes equal allocation across the \(J\) groups named by c_weights and a pooled error term on \(N - J\) degrees of freedom. Groups with zero weight still contribute error degrees of freedom, which is why they belong in c_weights when the fitted model will include them. Planning for a paired design counts units. Each condition is observed on every unit, so the answer is the total sample size \(N\), and the mean of the \(N\) per-unit contrast scores has standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\) on \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom, where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the scores. That standard deviation carries the correlation between the measures (see the paired designs paragraph of power_equivalence_c), and a positive correlation is what lets a paired design reach a given power with fewer observations than independent groups need.

The search. The function starts from the normal-theory approximation and moves to the smallest integer size (per group, or the number of units of a paired design) whose exact power reaches desired_power. Power is monotone in the size once the design is feasible, so the search is a short walk.

Relation to the half-width rule. With symmetric bounds \(\pm\delta\), true_contrast = 0, and \(\alpha = .05\), targeting a 90% CI half-width of \(\delta/2\) yields a declaration probability of about .90; this function makes the probability the target directly rather than through the width.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

Schuirmann, D. J. (1987). A comparison of the two one-sided tests procedure and the power approach for assessing the equivalence of average bioavailability. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 15(6), 657–680.

Examples

# 1. Two-group equivalence with bounds of 5 raw-scale points and an
#    anticipated error SD of 15.67: n per group for 90% power at
#    true equivalence.
ss_power_equivalence_c(c_weights = c(1, -1), true_sd = 15.67,
                       contrast_upper = 5, desired_power = 0.90)
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 214  
#>  total_N               428  
#>  actual_power          0.901

# 2. Noninferiority is cheaper than equivalence at the same bound.
ss_power_equivalence_c(c_weights = c(1, -1), true_sd = 15.67,
                       contrast_upper = 5, desired_power = 0.90,
                       side = "noninferiority")
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 169  
#>  total_N               338  
#>  actual_power          0.900

# 3. A true contrast off center raises the requirement.
ss_power_equivalence_c(c_weights = c(1, -1), true_sd = 15.67,
                       contrast_upper = 5, true_contrast = 2,
                       desired_power = 0.90)
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 468  
#>  total_N               936  
#>  actual_power          0.900

# 4. A paired noninferiority design: difference scores with an
#    anticipated SD of 1 and a margin of 0.5. Each unit is measured
#    under both conditions, so the answer is the number of units,
#    necessary_N.
ss_power_equivalence_c(true_sd = 1, contrast_lower = 0.5,
                       desired_power = 0.90, side = "noninferiority",
                       design = "paired")
#>  term         value
#>  necessary_N  36   
#>  actual_power 0.903
